**Arianna Stassinopoulos Huffington** ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")**Ariadnē-Anna Stasinopoúlou**; [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Αριάδνη-Άννα Στασινοπούλου, pronounced[[ariˈaðni ˈana stasinoˈpulu]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Greek "Help:IPA/Greek"); born July 15, 1950) is a Greek and American author, [syndicated columnist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syndicated_columnist "Syndicated columnist") and businesswoman.

She is a co-founder of _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_, the founder and CEO of [Thrive Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrive_Global "Thrive Global"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:1-1) and the author of fifteen books.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-2) She has been named in [_Time_ magazine's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)") list of the world's 100 most influential people[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-Forbes2020-3) and the _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ Most Powerful Women list.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:2-4) Huffington serves on numerous boards, including [Onex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onex_Corporation "Onex Corporation") and Global Citizen.

Two of her books have been dogged by allegations of [plagiarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagiarism "Plagiarism"), for one of which she paid another author an out-of-court settlement. Her last two books, _Thrive: The Third Metric to Redefining Success and Creating a Life of Well-Being, Wisdom, and Wonder_ and _The Sleep Revolution: Transforming Your Life, One Night at a Time_, both became international bestsellers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-5)

Huffington, the former wife of Republican congressman [Michael Huffington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Huffington "Michael Huffington"), co-founded _[The Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Huffington\_Post "The Huffington Post")_, which was later acquired by [BuzzFeed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed "BuzzFeed").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-6) She was a popular [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States "Conservatism in the United States") commentator in the mid-1990s, after which, in the late 1990s, she offered [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_liberalism_in_the_United_States "Modern liberalism in the United States") points of view in public, while remaining involved in business endeavors.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-7) In 2003, she ran as an [independent candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_candidate "Independent candidate") for [governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_California "Governor of California") in the [California recall election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_California_recall_election "2003 California recall election") and lost.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-8) In 2009, Huffington was No.12 in _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ first-ever list of the Most Influential Women In Media.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-9) She has also moved up to No.42 in _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_'s Top 100 in Media List.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-10) As of 2014, she was listed by _Forbes_ as the 52nd Most Powerful Woman in the World.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-11) She had moved to 77th as of 2018 and dropped off the list as of 2019.

In 2011, [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") acquired _The Huffington Post_ for US$315 million and made Huffington the president and [editor-in-chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Editor-in-chief "Editor-in-chief") of The Huffington Post Media Group, which included _The Huffington Post_ and then-existing AOL properties including [AOL Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL_Music "AOL Music"), [Engadget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engadget "Engadget"), [Patch Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patch_Media "Patch Media"), and StyleList.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-AOL_Press_Release-12)

She stepped down from her role at _The Huffington Post_ in August 2016 to focus on a new start-up, [Thrive Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrive_Global "Thrive Global"), a behavior-change technology company with the mission of improving productivity and health outcomes.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-13)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Huffington was born Ariadnē-Anna Stasinopoúlou (Αριάδνη-Άννα Στασινοπούλου) in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens"), Greece,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:2-4) in 1950,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-14) the daughter of Konstantinos (a journalist and management consultant) and Elli (née Georgiadi) Stasinopoulou,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-yaya/19990222-15) and is the sister of Agapi (an author, speaker, and performer).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-Silverman-16) She moved to the United Kingdom at the age of 16 and studied [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") at [Girton College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girton_College,_Cambridge "Girton College, Cambridge"), where she was the first foreign, and third female,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-Talbot,_Margaret_1998_page_40-47-17)[president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Cambridge_Union_Society_presidents "List of Cambridge Union Society presidents") of the [Cambridge Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Union "Cambridge Union").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-18) She studied abroad in India, and told IANS in an email interview "India has long held a special place in my heart, from the time I went to study comparative religion at [Visva-Bharati University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visva-Bharati_University "Visva-Bharati University")."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-19)

In 1971, Huffington appeared in an edition of _[Face the Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face\_the\_Music\_(UK\_TV\_programme) "Face the Music (UK TV programme)")_ along with [Bernard Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Levin "Bernard Levin"). A relationship developed, of which she wrote, after his death: "He wasn't just the big love of my life, he was a mentor as a writer and a role model as a thinker."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-arianna-20) Huffington began writing books in the 1970s, with editorial help from Levin.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-22) The two traveled to music festivals around the world for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"). They spent summers patronizing three-star restaurants in France. At the age of 30, she remained deeply in love with him but longed to have children; Levin never wanted to marry or have children.

From March to April 1980, Huffington joined [Bob Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Langley "Bob Langley") as the co-host of [BBC1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC1 "BBC1")'s late-night talk and entertainment show _Saturday Night at the Mill_, appearing in just five editions before being dropped from the programme.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-23)

In 1973, Arianna (as Stasinopoúlou) wrote a book titled _The Female Woman_, attacking the Women's Liberation movement in general and [Germaine Greer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germaine_Greer "Germaine Greer")'s 1970 _[The Female Eunuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Female\_Eunuch "The Female Eunuch")_ in particular. In the book she wrote, "Women's Lib claims that the achievement of total liberation would transform the lives of all women for the better; the truth is that it would transform only the lives of women with strong lesbian tendencies."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:3-24)

In the late 1980s, Huffington wrote several articles for _[National Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Review "National Review")_. In 1981, she wrote a biography of [Maria Callas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Callas "Maria Callas"), _Maria Callas – The Woman Behind the Legend_, and in 1989, a biography of [Pablo Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Picasso "Pablo Picasso"), _Picasso: Creator and Destroyer_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-25)

Huffington rose to the national U.S. prominence during the unsuccessful Senate bid in 1994 by her then husband, Michael Huffington, a [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"). She became known as a reliable supporter of conservative causes such as [Newt Gingrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newt_Gingrich "Newt Gingrich")'s "[Republican Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Revolution "Republican Revolution")" and [Bob Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dole "Bob Dole")'s 1996 [candidacy for president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_presidential_election "1996 United States presidential election"). She teamed up with [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism")[comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedian "Comedian")[Al Franken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Franken "Al Franken") as the conservative half of "Strange Bedfellows"[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-26) during [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central")'s coverage of the 1996 U.S. presidential election. For her work, she and the writing team of _[Politically Incorrect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politically\_Incorrect "Politically Incorrect")_ were nominated for a 1997 [Emmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy "Emmy") for Outstanding Writing for a Variety or Music Program.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-27)

As late as 1998, Huffington still aligned herself with the Republican Party. During that year, she did a weekly radio show in Los Angeles called _[Left, Right & Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left,\_Right\_&\_Center "Left, Right & Center")_, that "match[ed] her, the so-called 'right-winger', against self-described centrist policy wonk [Matt Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Miller_(journalist) "Matthew Miller (journalist)"), and veteran 'leftist' journalist [Robert Scheer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Scheer "Robert Scheer")."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-Talbot,_Margaret_1998_page_40-47-17)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-28) In an April 1998 profile in _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_, [Margaret Talbot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Talbot "Margaret Talbot") wrote, "Most recently, she has cast herself as a kind of Republican Spice Girl – an endearingly ditzy right wing gal-about-town who is a guilty pleasure for people who know better." Huffington described herself by side-stepping the traditional party divide, saying "the right–left divisions are so outdated now. For me, the primary division is between people who are aware of what I call 'the two nations' (rich and poor), and those who are not."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-Talbot,_Margaret_1998_page_40-47-17)

Huffington, of Greek background, opposed the [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") intervention in [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia "Serbia") during the [Yugoslav Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslav_Wars "Yugoslav Wars")[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-29) and in 2000, she co-convened the "Shadow Conventions",[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-30) which appeared at the [Republican National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Republican_National_Convention "2000 Republican National Convention") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") and the [Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Democratic_National_Convention "2000 Democratic National Convention") in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") at [Patriotic Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hope_Patriotic_Hall "Bob Hope Patriotic Hall").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-31)

Huffington headed [The Detroit Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Detroit_Project "The Detroit Project"), a public interest group [lobbying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbying "Lobbying") automakers to start producing cars running on [alternative fuels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_fuel "Alternative fuel"). The project's 2003 TV ads, which equated driving [sport utility vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_utility_vehicle "Sport utility vehicle") to funding [terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism "Terrorism"), proved to be particularly controversial, with some stations refusing to run them.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-32)

In a 2004 appearance on _[The Daily Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Show "The Daily Show")_ with [Jon Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Stewart "Jon Stewart"), she announced her endorsement of [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") by saying, "When your house is burning down, you don't worry about the remodeling."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-33) Huffington was a panel speaker during the 2005 California Democratic Party State Convention, held in Los Angeles. She also spoke at the 2004 [College Democrats of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Democrats_of_America "College Democrats of America") Convention in Boston, which was held in conjunction with the [2004 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Democratic_National_Convention "2004 Democratic National Convention"). She was also a regular panelist on the nationally syndicated weekend radio program, _Both Sides Now with Huffington & Matalin_,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-bothsides-34) hosted by [Mark Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Green_(New_York_politician) "Mark Green (New York politician)").

Huffington serves on the board of directors of the [Berggruen Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berggruen_Institute "Berggruen Institute"),[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-35) the [Center for Public Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Public_Integrity "Center for Public Integrity"),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-36)[Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber "Uber"),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-37) and [Onex Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onex_Corporation "Onex Corporation").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-38)

She is also a One Young World Counsellor, speaking to delegates at summits in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), in 2013 and [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland"), in 2014. She spoke about her "third metric" for success and the value of youth leadership.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-39)

### _The Huffington Post_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The Huffington Post")]

In 2005, Huffington founded _[The Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_ (now known as _HuffPost_) with[Andrew Breitbart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart "Andrew Breitbart"), [Kenneth Lerer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Lerer "Kenneth Lerer"), and [Jonah Peretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Peretti "Jonah Peretti").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-46) It was launched on May 9, 2005, as a commentary outlet, blog, and an alternative to news aggregators such as the _[Drudge Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drudge\_Report "Drudge Report")_. The site historically published work from both paid staff writers and reporters and unpaid bloggers.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-47) In February 2011, [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") acquired _The Huffington Post_ for US$315 million, making Huffington editor-in-chief of The Huffington Post Media Group.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-48) In 2012, _The Huffington Post_ became the first commercially run United States digital media enterprise to win a [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-49) In 2016, Huffington left _The Huffington Post_.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-huffingtongone-50)

### Thrive Global

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Thrive Global")]

Main article: [Thrive Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrive_Global "Thrive Global")

In 2016 Huffington stepped down from her positions at AOL and _Huffington Post_ to launch her new enterprise, Thrive Global, which claims to offer "science-based solutions" to end stress and burnout.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-51)

*   **Meditative Story Podcast** – In August 2019, Thrive Global launched the podcast [Meditative Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditative_Story "Meditative Story") in partnership with WaitWhat – a media company led by former TED executives [June Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_Cohen "June Cohen") and Deron Triff. The podcast supposedly combines first-person stories with meditation prompts and original music to create a "mindfulness experience" in audio.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-52)_[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ has described it as "part first-person narrative podcast and part guided meditation."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-53)_Forbes_ has described it as "a completely new kind of listening experience that blends intimate first-person stories with mindfulness prompts, enveloped in beautiful music composition."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:0-54) Huffington described Meditative Story as "a response to a deep cultural need in our hyper sped up world to have a moment to recharge. The podcast is a tool-set for wellness combining intimate storytelling, that we’re all hardwired to respond to, plus moments of reflection."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:0-54) The podcast's first season featured stories from [Krista Tippett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krista_Tippett "Krista Tippett") (host of the radio show [On Being](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Being "On Being")), NPR Host [Peter Sagal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Sagal "Peter Sagal"), travel writer [Pico Iyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pico_Iyer "Pico Iyer"), LinkedIn cofounder [Reid Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid_Hoffman "Reid Hoffman"), Beautycon Media's [Moj Mahdara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moj_Mahdara "Moj Mahdara"), actor [Josh Radnor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Radnor "Josh Radnor"), and astronomer [Michelle Thaller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Thaller "Michelle Thaller"), among others.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-55)
*   **Thrive Global Podcast** – In 2017, Thrive Global launched a podcast with iHeart Radio featuring Huffington as host.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-56)

### California recall election participation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: California recall election participation")]

Huffington was an [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_independent "Political independent") candidate in the [2003 California gubernatorial recall election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_California_gubernatorial_recall_election "2003 California gubernatorial recall election") of California Governor [Gray Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gray_Davis "Gray Davis"). She described her candidacy against frontrunner [Arnold Schwarzenegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schwarzenegger "Arnold Schwarzenegger") as "the [hybrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_car "Hybrid car") versus the [Hummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hummer "Hummer")", making reference to her ownership of a hybrid vehicle, the [Toyota Prius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Prius "Toyota Prius"), and Schwarzenegger's Hummer. The two would proceed to have a high-profile clash during the election's [debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debate "Debate").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-57)

She dropped out of the race on September 30, 2003, and endorsed Governor Gray Davis' campaign to vote against the recall. Polls showed that only about 2 percent of California voters planned to vote for her at the time of her withdrawal.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-58) In the announcement of her withdrawal, Huffington stated,

> "It has become clear to me that the only way to stop a Republican takeover of our state is to vote No on the recall. Because it's also clear that I am not going to win on October 7, I am withdrawing from the race so that I can devote all my time and energy in the remaining week to defeating the recall – and to defeating the Arnold Schwarzenegger-[Pete Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Wilson "Pete Wilson") forces that are trying to use the recall to hijack our state."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-59)

Though she failed to stop the recall, Huffington's name remained on the ballot and she [placed 5th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_California_recall_election#Results "2003 California recall election"), capturing 47,505 votes – less than 1% of the vote.

### Presence in media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Presence in media")]

Huffington was a panelist on the weekly [BBC Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4") political discussion programme _[Any Questions?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Any\_Questions%3F "Any Questions?")_, and the BBC television panel games _[Call My Bluff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call\_My\_Bluff\_(UK\_game\_show) "Call My Bluff (UK game show)")_ and _[Face the Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face\_the\_Music\_(UK\_TV\_programme) "Face the Music (UK TV programme)")_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-60) She served as co-host of BBC's late-night chat show _Saturday Night at the Mill_ for four weeks before viewer complaints caused her to be dropped from the show.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-61) Huffington at one point was the co-host of the weekly, nationally syndicated [public radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_radio "Public radio") program _Both Sides Now_, along with [Mary Matalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Matalin "Mary Matalin"), former top aide to the [George W. Bush administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_George_W._Bush "Presidency of George W. Bush"). Every week on _Both Sides Now_, Huffington and Matalin discussed the nation's relevant political issues, offering both sides of every issue to listeners. _Both Sides Now_ was hosted by former [Air America Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_America_Radio "Air America Radio") president and _HuffPost_ blogger [Mark Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Green_(New_York_politician) "Mark Green (New York politician)").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-bothsides-34)

Prior to _The Huffington Post_, Huffington hosted a website called AriannaOnline.com. Her first foray onto the internet was a website called Resignation.com, which called for the resignation of President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") and was a rallying place for conservatives opposing Clinton. About Clinton resigning, she wrote, "Only some act of sacrifice can begin to restore the image of the President that we are left with from the [Starr report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starr_report "Starr report") – a man of staggering [narcissism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narcissism "Narcissism") and self-indulgence, whom nobody dared gainsay, investing his energies first in gratifying his sexual greeds and then in using his staff, his friends, and the Secret Service to cover up the truth."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-62)

In November 2008, Huffington joined the cast of [Seth MacFarlane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_MacFarlane "Seth MacFarlane")'s animated series _[The Cleveland Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cleveland\_Show "The Cleveland Show")_, where she lent her voice to the wife of [Tim the Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_the_Bear "Tim the Bear"), also named [Arianna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Cleveland_Show_characters#Arianna_the_Bear "List of The Cleveland Show characters").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-63)

Huffington was spoofed by actress [Tracey Ullman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracey_Ullman "Tracey Ullman") in her [Showtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showtime_(TV_network) "Showtime (TV network)") comedy series _[Tracey Ullman's State of the Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracey\_Ullman's\_State\_of\_the\_Union "Tracey Ullman's State of the Union")_. Huffington spoke glowingly of the impersonation.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:3-24)

Huffington was further impersonated by actresses [Michaela Watkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michaela_Watkins "Michaela Watkins") and [Nasim Pedrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasim_Pedrad "Nasim Pedrad") on _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-64)

She appeared as herself in the May 10, 2010, episode of the [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") sitcom _[How I Met Your Mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How\_I\_Met\_Your\_Mother "How I Met Your Mother")_.

Huffington participated in the 24th annual "Distinguished Speaker Series" at the [University at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo "University at Buffalo"), New York, on September 16, 2010. She headlined a debate against radio co-host Mary Matalin on current world events, political issues, and the local Buffalo economy. The University at Buffalo "Distinguished Speaker Series" has featured a multitude of world-renowned politicians and celebrities such as [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair"), [Bill Nye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Nye "Bill Nye"), [Jon Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Stewart "Jon Stewart"), and [the Dalai Lama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dalai_Lama "The Dalai Lama").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-65)

Huffington offered to provide as many buses as necessary to transport those who wanted to go to Jon Stewart's [Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rally_to_Restore_Sanity_and/or_Fear "Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear") on October 30, 2010, from _The Huffington Post_ headquarters in New York City.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-66) Ultimately, she paid for 150 buses to ferry almost 10,000 people from [Citi Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citi_Field "Citi Field") in Queens to [RFK Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RFK_Stadium "RFK Stadium") in DC.

Huffington played herself in the _[Family Guy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family\_Guy "Family Guy")_ episode "[Brian Writes a Bestseller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Writes_a_Bestseller "Brian Writes a Bestseller")" along with [Dana Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dana_Gould "Dana Gould") and [Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher "Bill Maher") in a [live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_action "Live action") segment of _[Real Time with Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real\_Time\_with\_Bill\_Maher "Real Time with Bill Maher")_.

In 2012, Huffington became a [LinkedIn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LinkedIn "LinkedIn") influencer, writing about success and sharing professional insights.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-67)

## Claims of plagiarism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Claims of plagiarism")]

Huffington was accused of [plagiarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagiarism "Plagiarism") for copying material for her book _Maria Callas_ (1981); the claims were settled out of court in 1981, with Callas' biographer Gerald Fitzgerald being paid "in the low five figures."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-Orth,_Maureen_2005_Page_117-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-70)

## Religious views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Religious views")]

Huffington has had a lifelong interest in spirituality; in her youth, together with Bernard Levin, she explored the [Rajneesh movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajneesh_movement "Rajneesh movement"), later dating [Erhard Seminars Training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erhard_Seminars_Training "Erhard Seminars Training") founder [Werner Erhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Erhard "Werner Erhard") and going on to become affiliated with [John-Roger Hinkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John-Roger_Hinkins "John-Roger Hinkins")' [Movement of Spiritual Inner Awareness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_of_Spiritual_Inner_Awareness "Movement of Spiritual Inner Awareness").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:3-24)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-71) In 1994, she published a self-help book titled _The Fourth Instinct_, outlining her view that people should rise above the three basic instincts of survival, power, and sex to find their higher and better selves.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-vanessa-g-nymag-72)

## Awards and honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Awards and honors")]

Huffington was named to the 2011 Time 100 as a media mogul.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-73) Huffington was selected for the inaugural 2021 [Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes") 50 Over 50; made up of entrepreneurs, leaders, scientists and creators who are over the age of 50.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-74)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arianna_Huffington&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Huffington is Greek by birth[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-vanessa-g-nymag-72) and became a [naturalized American citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalized_American_citizen "Naturalized American citizen") in 1990.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-75) She met her husband [Michael Huffington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Huffington "Michael Huffington") in 1985.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-76) They were married a year later, on April 12, 1986,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-77) and have two daughters.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-78)

The couple later moved to [Santa Barbara, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Barbara,_California "Santa Barbara, California"), and, in 1992, Michael ran as a Republican for a seat in the [U.S. House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives"), winning the election by a significant margin. In 1994, he [narrowly lost the race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_United_States_Senate_election_in_California "1994 United States Senate election in California") for the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") seat in California to incumbent [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-79)

The couple divorced in 1997.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-80) In 1998, Michael Huffington shared that he was [bisexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bisexual "Bisexual"), saying, "I know now that my sexuality is part of who I am, I've been through a long process of finding out the truth about me."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-82) He stated, "In December 1985, in my Houston townhouse I sat down with [Arianna] and told her that I had dated women and men so that she would be aware of it... The good news was that it was not an issue for her."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-:3-24)

Huffington has residences in New York City, with her sister, Agapi Stassinopoulos,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-Silverman-16) and the [Brentwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentwood,_Los_Angeles "Brentwood, Los Angeles") neighborhood of Los Angeles.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianna_Huffington#cite_note-85)

# Arianna Huffington to leave Huffington Post for startup Thrive

This article is more than 10 years old

Founder of digital publisher says she wants to focus on health-themed project as she has become ‘obsessed’ with reducing impact of stress on daily life

[Jasper Jackson](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/jasper-jackson) in London and [Sam Thielman](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/sam-thielman) in New York

Thu 11 Aug 2016 08.20 EDT Last modified on Tue 28 Nov 2017 11.34 EST

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

Media mogul turned self-help guru [Arianna Huffington](https://www.theguardian.com/media/ariannahuffington) is to leave the Huffington Post to launch a health-focused startup called Thrive Global to tackle stress and burnout.

Eleven years after Huffington co-founded the site that bears her name, and has changed the face of journalism, the site’s editor-in-chief and president, told staff on Thursday that she would be giving up her role at the media company after closing a funding round for Thrive late last week.

[![Image 3: Arianna Huffington at home in NYC for the Observer Magazine 1/11/16](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5d873dcb2456c57df4068f82f5ea40afbd4c820b/0_326_5760_3456/5760.jpg?width=460&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=d1b61b9579b9386a908a2b7ebd2b34ad) Arianna Huffington: from bedroom to boardroom with the Uber woman Read more](https://www.theguardian.com/media/2016/may/01/arianna-huffington-uber-directors-huffington-post)

She said in a statement: “When I decided to create Thrive Global, I thought it would be possible to build a startup and continue as editor-in-chief of the Huffington Post. Today, it’s clear that was an illusion.

“As Thrive Global moved from an idea to a reality, with investors, staff, and offices, it became clear to me that I simply couldn’t do justice to both companies.”

In a memo to staff, Huffington said she had “become more and more passionate – okay, obsessed – with burnout and stress and how we can reduce their impact on our lives”.

Her departure comes just over a decade after she founded the Huffington Post with Kenneth Lerer, Jonah Peretti and Andrew Breitbart, who would also go on to be among the most influential media figures of their generation. Peretti founded BuzzFeed and Lerer is its chairman, while Breitbart went on to create the rightwing news site that is named after him.

Kate Palmer, editorial director of lifestyle for the Huffington Post, told the Guardian the staff would be hearing about succession plans in an 11am meeting on Thursday. “Obviously it’s a bittersweet day, but HuffPo is poised to be an incredible leader in this space, and we’re not gonna miss a beat,” Palmer said.

In 2011 Huffington Post was bought for $315m (£243m) by AOL, which in turn was bought for $4.4bn in 2014 by US mobile operator Verizon. Verizon recently [added Yahoo](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/jul/25/yahoo-to-sell-core-web-business-to-verizon) to its portfolio, buying the ailing internet giant for $4.83bn (£3.62bn) in July.

Traffic to HuffPo’s sites has dropped precipitously this year: according to data from web analytics firm comScore, global audience fell 23% from June 2015 to June 2016.

Born Ariadnē-Anna Stasinopoúlou in Athens in 1950, Huffington rose to prominence in the 1990s as a conservative Republican presence on television, on the radio and in her now ex-husband Michael Huffington’s bid for one of California’s Senate seats in 1994. She appeared in Comedy Central’s coverage of the 1996 US elections as “the beautiful but evil Arianna Huffington” alongside “the talented but smug Al Franken” in a segment called Strange Bedfellows. Franken is now a Democratic US senator.

But for her namesake enterprise Huffington made a Damascene conversion. The site was tactically liberal from the get-go and originally envisioned as a competitor to conservative links page The Drudge Report. The Huffington Post pioneered a brand of journalism that has come to typify much of the digital news world – often aggregated from work from other outlets, sometimes without attribution or [permission](https://www.theguardian.com/media/2015/oct/28/cartoonist-the-oatmeal-trolls-huffpo-over-images-published-sans-permission), with the majority of its original material produced by unpaid contributors, famous or otherwise.

In a June 2012 piece in the Columbia Journalism Review, Columbia journalism school professor Michael Shapiro [characterized the site’s success](http://www.cjr.org/cover_story/six_degrees_of_aggregation.php) as a combination of rapid popularity, low overhead and the level of access afforded to Huffington by her years in politics and on television. The site pitched famous people a popular platform from which they could opine, which was better than money; to its unpaid low-level staffers, it dangled the prestige of appearing in print next to the famous ones.

“[I]t was up to Huffington to find the bloggers,” Shapiro wrote. “She wanted Arthur Schlesinger; he was a friend. So was Larry David. And John Cusack. And Harry Shearer.”

“When somebody writes something for us, we know it’s real, we know they want to write it,” HuffPo UK editor-in-chief Steve Hull told Radio 4 earlier this year, by way of defending the company’s practice of refusing to pay many of its writers. “It’s not been forced or paid for. I think that’s something to be proud of.”

After Huffington’s departure announcement, AOL CEO Tim Armstrong said the company remained committed to the Huffington Post, and looked forward to partnering with Thrive.

He said: “Arianna is a visionary who built the Huffington Post into a truly transformative news platform. Today, The Huffington Post is a firmly established and celebrated news source and AOL and Verizon are committed to continuing its growth and the groundbreaking work Arianna pioneered.”

Though she stayed on as the site’s editor-in-chief and president following Huffington Post’s changes of ownership, Huffington has in recent years spent increasing amounts of time promoting healthy living concepts such as mindfulness and the benefits of getting enough sleep. In her memo to staff she joked she would remain HuffPo’s “unofficial Sleep Ombudsman”.

Thrive, which shares a name with a book published by Huffington in 2014, promises to offer a range of services and support using “the latest scientific findings from experts in the fields of neuroscience, psychology, productivity, sports and sleep”.

The company is backed by a range of venture capital firms and angel investors led by Lerer’s Lerer Hippeau Ventures, and has been running a pilot programme with Accenture.

Huffington, who will serve as its chief executive, added: “As Thrive Global moved from an idea to a reality, with investors, staff, and offices, it became clear to me that I simply couldn’t do justice to both companies ... Running both companies would have involved working around the clock, which would be a betrayal of the very principles of Thrive I’ve been writing and speaking about.”

“I step down as editor-in-chief filled with gratitude for our amazing [HuffPost](https://www.theguardian.com/media/huffington-post) team and for what we’ve built together, and for Tim Armstrong who had the vision to buy HuffPost five years ago and to support from day one our global expansion. The journey of the last 11 years has exceeded my wildest expectations. I’m proud of all we’ve accomplished and very confident about HuffPost’s future with the strongest leadership team we’ve ever had and the full support of AOL and Verizon.”

According to a leading global watchdog, US democracy is now more imperiled than at any point since the 1960s. Press freedom is under threat on many fronts – from criminal investigations to politicized regulation, frivolous lawsuits and catastrophic funding cuts to public media.

With the midterm elections approaching, these attacks are accelerating. Most recently, Donald Trump banned CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, in retaliation for “negative” coverage.

In August, Trump suggested that the host of Meet the Press should be “punished” by the FCC for making a factual statement he disliked. Trump is using the agency – which is supposed to be an independent regulator – to settle political scores: The FCC targeted ABC after Jimmy Kimmel made a joke about Melania Trump.

The Pentagon fired the editor of Stars and Stripes newspaper for “insubordination” shortly after they reported on a suicide attempt aboard the USS Lincoln.

Together these efforts make it more difficult to get fact-based reporting to US voters ahead of critical elections that will determine control of Congress and the future of Trump’s agenda.

Making matters worse, many of the US’s largest news organizations are now owned by billionaires whose personal and business interests may be at odds with safeguarding editorial independence. Media critics have observed how CBS News, now owned by a Trump ally, has softened its coverage; CNN could be taken over by the same billionaire; and Jeff Bezos has imposed extreme staff cuts and editorial interventions at the Washington Post.

When freedom is under attack, it falls to a determined few news organizations to ensure the full truth still reaches the public. The Guardian is owned neither by a billionaire nor a corporation and remains dedicated to keeping trustworthy journalism paywall-free for the world.

**Despite the risks of maintaining our fierce independence, what sustains us – and fills us with deep gratitude – is the unwavering support we’ve seen from readers. # Arianna Huffington to leave Huffington Post for startup Thrive

This article is more than 10 years old

Founder of digital publisher says she wants to focus on health-themed project as she has become ‘obsessed’ with reducing impact of stress on daily life

[Jasper Jackson](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/jasper-jackson) in London and [Sam Thielman](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/sam-thielman) in New York

Thu 11 Aug 2016 08.20 EDT Last modified on Tue 28 Nov 2017 11.34 EST

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

Media mogul turned self-help guru [Arianna Huffington](https://www.theguardian.com/media/ariannahuffington) is to leave the Huffington Post to launch a health-focused startup called Thrive Global to tackle stress and burnout.

Eleven years after Huffington co-founded the site that bears her name, and has changed the face of journalism, the site’s editor-in-chief and president, told staff on Thursday that she would be giving up her role at the media company after closing a funding round for Thrive late last week.

[![Image 3: Arianna Huffington at home in NYC for the Observer Magazine 1/11/16](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5d873dcb2456c57df4068f82f5ea40afbd4c820b/0_326_5760_3456/5760.jpg?width=460&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=d1b61b9579b9386a908a2b7ebd2b34ad) Arianna Huffington: from bedroom to boardroom with the Uber woman Read more](https://www.theguardian.com/media/2016/may/01/arianna-huffington-uber-directors-huffington-post)

She said in a statement: “When I decided to create Thrive Global, I thought it would be possible to build a startup and continue as editor-in-chief of the Huffington Post. Today, it’s clear that was an illusion.

“As Thrive Global moved from an idea to a reality, with investors, staff, and offices, it became clear to me that I simply couldn’t do justice to both companies.”

In a memo to staff, Huffington said she had “become more and more passionate – okay, obsessed – with burnout and stress and how we can reduce their impact on our lives”.

Her departure comes just over a decade after she founded the Huffington Post with Kenneth Lerer, Jonah Peretti and Andrew Breitbart, who would also go on to be among the most influential media figures of their generation. Peretti founded BuzzFeed and Lerer is its chairman, while Breitbart went on to create the rightwing news site that is named after him.

Kate Palmer, editorial director of lifestyle for the Huffington Post, told the Guardian the staff would be hearing about succession plans in an 11am meeting on Thursday. “Obviously it’s a bittersweet day, but HuffPo is poised to be an incredible leader in this space, and we’re not gonna miss a beat,” Palmer said.

In 2011 Huffington Post was bought for $315m (£243m) by AOL, which in turn was bought for $4.4bn in 2014 by US mobile operator Verizon. Verizon recently [added Yahoo](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/jul/25/yahoo-to-sell-core-web-business-to-verizon) to its portfolio, buying the ailing internet giant for $4.83bn (£3.62bn) in July.

Traffic to HuffPo’s sites has dropped precipitously this year: according to data from web analytics firm comScore, global audience fell 23% from June 2015 to June 2016.

Born Ariadnē-Anna Stasinopoúlou in Athens in 1950, Huffington rose to prominence in the 1990s as a conservative Republican presence on television, on the radio and in her now ex-husband Michael Huffington’s bid for one of California’s Senate seats in 1994. She appeared in Comedy Central’s coverage of the 1996 US elections as “the beautiful but evil Arianna Huffington” alongside “the talented but smug Al Franken” in a segment called Strange Bedfellows. Franken is now a Democratic US senator.

But for her namesake enterprise Huffington made a Damascene conversion. The site was tactically liberal from the get-go and originally envisioned as a competitor to conservative links page The Drudge Report. The Huffington Post pioneered a brand of journalism that has come to typify much of the digital news world – often aggregated from work from other outlets, sometimes without attribution or [permission](https://www.theguardian.com/media/2015/oct/28/cartoonist-the-oatmeal-trolls-huffpo-over-images-published-sans-permission), with the majority of its original material produced by unpaid contributors, famous or otherwise.

In a June 2012 piece in the Columbia Journalism Review, Columbia journalism school professor Michael Shapiro [characterized the site’s success](http://www.cjr.org/cover_story/six_degrees_of_aggregation.php) as a combination of rapid popularity, low overhead and the level of access afforded to Huffington by her years in politics and on television. The site pitched famous people a popular platform from which they could opine, which was better than money; to its unpaid low-level staffers, it dangled the prestige of appearing in print next to the famous ones.

“[I]t was up to Huffington to find the bloggers,” Shapiro wrote. “She wanted Arthur Schlesinger; he was a friend. So was Larry David. And John Cusack. And Harry Shearer.”

“When somebody writes something for us, we know it’s real, we know they want to write it,” HuffPo UK editor-in-chief Steve Hull told Radio 4 earlier this year, by way of defending the company’s practice of refusing to pay many of its writers. “It’s not been forced or paid for. I think that’s something to be proud of.”

After Huffington’s departure announcement, AOL CEO Tim Armstrong said the company remained committed to the Huffington Post, and looked forward to partnering with Thrive.

He said: “Arianna is a visionary who built the Huffington Post into a truly transformative news platform. Today, The Huffington Post is a firmly established and celebrated news source and AOL and Verizon are committed to continuing its growth and the groundbreaking work Arianna pioneered.”

Though she stayed on as the site’s editor-in-chief and president following Huffington Post’s changes of ownership, Huffington has in recent years spent increasing amounts of time promoting healthy living concepts such as mindfulness and the benefits of getting enough sleep. In her memo to staff she joked she would remain HuffPo’s “unofficial Sleep Ombudsman”.

Thrive, which shares a name with a book published by Huffington in 2014, promises to offer a range of services and support using “the latest scientific findings from experts in the fields of neuroscience, psychology, productivity, sports and sleep”.

The company is backed by a range of venture capital firms and angel investors led by Lerer’s Lerer Hippeau Ventures, and has been running a pilot programme with Accenture.

Huffington, who will serve as its chief executive, added: “As Thrive Global moved from an idea to a reality, with investors, staff, and offices, it became clear to me that I simply couldn’t do justice to both companies ... Running both companies would have involved working around the clock, which would be a betrayal of the very principles of Thrive I’ve been writing and speaking about.”

“I step down as editor-in-chief filled with gratitude for our amazing [HuffPost](https://www.theguardian.com/media/huffington-post) team and for what we’ve built together, and for Tim Armstrong who had the vision to buy HuffPost five years ago and to support from day one our global expansion. The journey of the last 11 years has exceeded my wildest expectations. I’m proud of all we’ve accomplished and very confident about HuffPost’s future with the strongest leadership team we’ve ever had and the full support of AOL and Verizon.”

**Andrew James Breitbart** ([/ˈ b r aɪ t b ɑːr t/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); February 1, 1969 – March 1, 2012) was an American [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States "Conservatism in the United States") journalist[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-c-span-1) and political commentator who was the founder of _[Breitbart News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breitbart\_News "Breitbart News")_ and a co-founder of _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-huff-2)

Breitbart played a central role in generating media coverage of the [Anthony Weiner sexting scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Weiner_sexting_scandals "Anthony Weiner sexting scandals"), the [firing of Shirley Sherrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firing_of_Shirley_Sherrod "Firing of Shirley Sherrod"), and the [ACORN 2009 undercover videos controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACORN_2009_undercover_videos_controversy "ACORN 2009 undercover videos controversy").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-3) Commenters such as [Nick Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Gillespie "Nick Gillespie") and [Conor Friedersdorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conor_Friedersdorf "Conor Friedersdorf") have credited Breitbart with changing how people wrote about politics by "show[ing] how the Internet could be used to route around information bottlenecks imposed by official spokesmen and legacy news outlets."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Atlantic1-5)

## Early life

Breitbart was born to Irish American parents in Los Angeles on February 1, 1969.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WAPO20120301-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-7) According to his birth certificate, his biological father was a folk singer. When he was three weeks old, he was adopted by Gerald and Arlene Breitbart, a restaurant owner and banker respectively, and grew up in the affluent neighborhood of [Brentwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentwood,_Los_Angeles "Brentwood, Los Angeles").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WAPO20120301-6) His adoptive family was [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews"); his mother had [converted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Judaism "Conversion to Judaism") to Judaism when marrying his father.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-wsj-9) Breitbart studied at [Hebrew school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_school "Hebrew school") and had a [Bar Mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_Mitzvah "Bar Mitzvah").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-10)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8)

Breitbart attended [Brentwood School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentwood_School_(Los_Angeles) "Brentwood School (Los Angeles)"), one of the country's top private schools, but did not distinguish himself, saying: "My sense of humor saved me".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8) However, he discovered that he loved writing, publishing his first comedic piece in the school newspaper, the _Brentwood Eagle_, analyzing the inequality in his high school's senior and junior parking lots: "One had Mercedes and BMWs, the other Sciroccos and GTIs".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8) Breitbart remembers his upbringing as apolitical, except in one instance: when the family's rabbi tried to defend [Jesse Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Jackson "Jesse Jackson") against charges of antisemitism after his "[Hymietown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymietown "Hymietown")" comment, his parents left the synagogue in protest.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8)

> [Joel Pollak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Pollak "Joel Pollak") wrote about how (Breitbart's) life and fire extended to Judaism: 'Andrew was proudly, and playfully, Jewish. In the last days of his life he wondered openly about observing [Shabbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabbat "Shabbat"), even as he continued to tease me about not eating bacon and shrimp cocktails. More than once he burst into a Hebrew school song or parts of his [bar mitzva portion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_and_bat_mitzvah#Aliyah_to_the_Torah "Bar and bat mitzvah") while working at his desk across from mine – partly to amuse me and partly to entertain himself.'[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-jpost.com-11)

Breitbart would remain "proudly and playfully Jewish" throughout his life. The liberal-Left Jewish weekly, _The Forward_, placed him on their 2010 list of the top 50 most influential American Jews.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-jpost.com-11) Joel Pollak wrote: "He carried his faith as he carried all his convictions: with a lighthearted touch but a deep commitment."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-jpost.com-11) Breitbart later said of his profession: "I'm glad I've become a journalist because I'd like to fight on behalf of the Israeli people... And the Israeli people, I adore and I love."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-jpost.com-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-12)

While in high school, Breitbart worked as a [pizza delivery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizza_delivery "Pizza delivery") driver; he sometimes delivered to celebrities such as [Judge Reinhold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judge_Reinhold "Judge Reinhold").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-13) He earned a [BA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in [American studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_studies "American studies") from [Tulane University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_University "Tulane University") in 1991, graduating with "no sense of [his] future whatsoever."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-14) His early jobs included a stint at [cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_television "Cable television") channel [E! Entertainment Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E!_Entertainment_Television "E! Entertainment Television"), working for the company's [online magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blog "Blog"), and some time in film production.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-wsj-9) He was a Lincoln Fellow at the [Claremont Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claremont_Institute "Claremont Institute") in 2009.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-16)

Previously left-leaning in his politics, Breitbart changed his political views after experiencing "an [epiphany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphany_(feeling) "Epiphany (feeling)")" while watching the late 1991 [confirmation hearings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas_Supreme_Court_nomination "Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination") for Supreme Court justice [Clarence Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas "Clarence Thomas"), due to what he considered unfounded attacks on the part of liberals based on former employee [Anita Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Hill "Anita Hill")'s sexual harassment accusations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-17) Breitbart later described himself as "a [Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") conservative" with [libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarianism "Libertarianism") sympathies.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-c-span-1)

Listening to radio hosts such as [Rush Limbaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush_Limbaugh "Rush Limbaugh") helped Breitbart refine his political and philosophical positions, igniting an interest in learning that he had suppressed as a result of his distaste for the "nihilistic musings of dead [critical theorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_theory "Critical theory")"[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Righteous_Indignation,_p._36-18) that had dominated his studies at Tulane. In this era, Breitbart also read [Camille Paglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Paglia "Camille Paglia")'s book _[Sexual Personae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual\_Personae "Sexual Personae")_ (1990), a massive survey of Western art, literature and culture from ancient Egypt to the 20th century, which, he wrote, "made me realize how little I really had learned in college."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Righteous_Indignation,_p._36-18)

## Public life

### Authorship, research, and reporting

Breitbart has been lauded for his role in the "evolution of pioneering websites" including _[The Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Huffington\_Post "The Huffington Post")_ and _[The Drudge Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drudge\_Report "Drudge Report")_, and later, for _[Breitbart News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breitbart\_News "Breitbart News")_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-19) Journalists such as [Nick Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Gillespie "Nick Gillespie") and [Conor Friedersdorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conor_Friedersdorf "Conor Friedersdorf") have credited Breitbart with bringing new voices to debates about politics and culture. Breitbart told _[Reason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason\_(magazine) "Reason (magazine)")_ in 2004 that, after feeling ignored by existing outlets, "We decided to go out and create our media." Described as "a series of do-it-yourself demonstration projects" and "conversation pits", the Breitbart websites have been both criticized and praised for their role in various political issues.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Atlantic1-5)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Gillespie-20) Breitbart has been recognized for adopting an inclusive stance with regard to the participation of gay people in the conservative movement. He has also been credited with helping to derail [conspiracy theories about Barack Obama's citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama_citizenship_conspiracy_theories "Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Atlantic1-5)

In 1995, Breitbart saw _The Drudge Report_ and was so impressed that he e-mailed [Matt Drudge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Drudge "Matt Drudge"). Breitbart said, "I thought what he was doing was by far the coolest thing on the Internet. And I still do."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-huff-2) Breitbart described himself as "Matt Drudge's [bitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitch_(insult)#In_reference_to_men "Bitch (insult)")"[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-biyatch-21) and selected and posted links to other news wire sources. Later, Drudge introduced him to a then still-[Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)")Arianna Huffington[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-wsj-9) and Breitbart subsequently assisted in the creation of _The Huffington Post_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-22)

Breitbart wrote a weekly column for _[The Washington Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Times "The Washington Times")_, which also appeared at [Real Clear Politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Clear_Politics "Real Clear Politics"). Breitbart also co-wrote the book _[Hollywood, Interrupted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,\_Interrupted "Hollywood, Interrupted"): Insanity Chic in Babylon_ with [Mark Ebner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Ebner "Mark Ebner"), a book that is highly critical of U.S. [celebrity culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_culture "Celebrity culture").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-23) On January 19, 2011, the [conservative gay rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_conservatism "LGBT conservatism") group [GOProud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GOProud "GOProud") announced Breitbart had joined its Advisory Council.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-24)

In 2011, Grand Central Publishing released Breitbart's book _Righteous Indignation: Excuse Me While I Save the World_,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-25) in which he discussed his own political evolution and the part he took in the rise of [new media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_media "New media"), most notably at the Drudge Report and _The Huffington Post_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-27)

### _Breitbart News_

Main article: [Breitbart News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breitbart_News "Breitbart News")

Breitbart launched his first website as a news site; it is often linked to by the _[Drudge Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drudge\_Report "Drudge Report")_ and other websites. It has wire stories from the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press"), [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters"), [Agence France-Presse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agence_France-Presse "Agence France-Presse"), [Fox News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News "Fox News"), [PR Newswire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PR_Newswire "PR Newswire"), and [U.S. Newswire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Newswire "U.S. Newswire"), as well as direct links to a number of major international newspapers. Its political viewpoint as well as its audience runs to the [right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing "Right-wing") within the U.S. political spectrum.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-28) In 2007, Breitbart launched a video blog, Breitbart.tv.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-29)

In February 2011, Breitbart and one of his editors [Larry O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_O'Connor_(radio_host) "Larry O'Connor (radio host)") were sued for [defamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamation "Defamation") by [Shirley Sherrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Sherrod "Shirley Sherrod"), who had been [fired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firing_of_Shirley_Sherrod "Firing of Shirley Sherrod") after Breitbart posted a video of a speech given by Sherrod. The video had been selectively edited to suggest that she had purposely discriminated against a white farmer, while in reality the unedited video told the story of how she had helped that farmer.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Gerstein-31) Breitbart himself maintained that he stated this in his article about it, and that the purpose of the video was to show the crowd's positive reaction to Sherrod's statements about discriminating against the white farmer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-32) In July 2015, it was reported that Sherrod and Breitbart's estate had reached a tentative settlement.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Gerstein-31) It was reported October 1, 2016, that the lawsuit was settled.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-33)

In June 2011, Breitbart's websites broke the story that congressman [Anthony Weiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Weiner "Anthony Weiner") was [sending underage females revealing photographs of himself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Weiner_sexting_scandal "Anthony Weiner sexting scandal").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-34)

Since Breitbart's passing, under [Steve Bannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Bannon "Steve Bannon")'s leadership, _Breitbart News_ has become recognized as a [far-right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-right "Far-right")[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-FarRight-35) news and opinion website, which has been described as [misogynistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misogynistic "Misogynistic"), [xenophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenophobic "Xenophobic"), and [racist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism_in_the_United_States "Racism in the United States") by academics and journalists, notably The University of California Press.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-misogyny_xenophobia_racism-36)

### Commentaries

In 2009, Breitbart appeared as a commentator on _[Real Time with Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real\_Time\_with\_Bill\_Maher "Real Time with Bill Maher")_ and _[Dennis Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis\_Miller "Dennis Miller")_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-37) In 2004, he was a guest commentator on [Fox News Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News_Channel "Fox News Channel")'s morning show and frequently appeared as a guest panelist on [Fox News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News "Fox News")'s late night program, _[Red Eye w/ Greg Gutfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Eye\_(talk\_show) "Red Eye (talk show)")_. Breitbart also appeared as a commentator in the 2004 documentary _[Michael Moore Hates America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael\_Moore\_Hates\_America "Michael Moore Hates America")_.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-38)

On October 22, 2009, Breitbart appeared on the [C-SPAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-SPAN "C-SPAN") program _[Washington Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_Journal "Washington Journal")_. He gave his opinions on the mainstream media, Hollywood, the [Obama administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama "Presidency of Barack Obama") and his personal political views, having heated debates with several callers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-c-span-1)

In the hours immediately following Senator [Ted Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy "Ted Kennedy")'s death, Breitbart called Kennedy a "villain", a "duplicitous bastard", a "prick"[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-politico-39) and "a special pile of human excrement", adding, "Sorry, he destroyed lives. And he knew it," referring to Kennedy's actions during the [Chappaquiddick incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappaquiddick_incident "Chappaquiddick incident"), the [Robert Bork Supreme Court nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bork_Supreme_Court_nomination "Robert Bork Supreme Court nomination"), and the [Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas_Supreme_Court_nomination "Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-41)

In February 2010, Breitbart received the [Reed Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reed_Irvine "Reed Irvine")[Accuracy in Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accuracy_in_Media "Accuracy in Media") Award during the [Conservative Political Action Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Political_Action_Conference "Conservative Political Action Conference") in Washington, D.C. During his acceptance speech, he responded directly to accusations by _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ reporter Kate Zernike that [Jason Mattera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Mattera "Jason Mattera"), a young conservative activist, had been using "racial tones" in his [allusions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allusions "Allusions") to President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), and had spoken in a "[Chris Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Rock "Chris Rock") voice". From the podium, Breitbart called Zernike "a despicable human being" for having made such allegations about what, according to him, was just Mattera's Brooklyn accent.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-42) At the same conference, Breitbart was also filmed saying to journalist [Max Blumenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Blumenthal "Max Blumenthal") that he found him to be "a jerk" and "a despicable human being" over a blog entry in which Blumenthal accused Breitbart of employing a racist.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-43) Blumenthal was referring to [James O'Keefe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_O'Keefe "James O'Keefe") over his having attended a [Georgetown Law Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_Law_Center "Georgetown Law Center") discussion on race featuring Kevin Martin, [John Derbyshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Derbyshire "John Derbyshire"), and [Jared Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jared_Taylor "Jared Taylor"), the last of whom founded _[American Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Renaissance\_(magazine) "American Renaissance (magazine)")_, a white supremacist online magazine. Neither O'Keefe nor Breitbart endorsed Taylor's views.

In 2011, Breitbart said that "of course" [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") was not a conservative, adding:

> But this is a message to those candidates who are languishing at 2 percent and 3 percent within the Republican Party who are brand names in Washington, but the rest of the country don't know... celebrity is everything in this country. And if these guys don't learn how to play the media the way that Barack Obama played the media last election cycle and the way that Donald Trump is playing the election cycle, we're going to probably get a celebrity candidate.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WP.Aug.7.16-44)

These comments resurfaced after the controversy of Donald Trump hiring _[Breitbart News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breitbart\_News "Breitbart News")'_ executive chairman [Steve Bannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Bannon "Steve Bannon") to be his [White House Chief Strategist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Chief_Strategist "White House Chief Strategist").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WP.Aug.7.16-44)

### Activism

See also: [Tea Party movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_party_movement#Reports_of_slurs_at_health_care_reform_protests "Tea party movement")

Breitbart often appeared as a speaker at [Tea Party movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Party_movement "Tea Party movement") events across the U.S. For example, Breitbart was a speaker at the first National Tea Party Convention at Gaylord Opryland Hotel in Nashville on February 6, 2010.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-45) Breitbart later involved himself in a controversy over allegations of [homophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophobia "Homophobia") and [racial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism") slurs being used at a March 20, 2010, rally at the [United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol") in Washington, D.C., by asserting that slurs were never used, and that "it was a set-up" by [Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi") and the Democratic Party. Breitbart offered to donate $100,000 to the [United Negro College Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Negro_College_Fund "United Negro College Fund") "for any audio/video footage of the [N-word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigger "Nigger") being hurled," claiming that the several Congressmen made it up. Breitbart insisted Congressman [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis "John Lewis") and several other witnesses were forced to lie, concluding that "Nancy Pelosi did a great disservice to a great civil rights icon by thrusting him out there to perform this mischievous task. His reputation is now on the line as a result of her desperation to take down the Tea Party movement."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-AB-100402-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WPost_Omb-47)

In February 2012, a YouTube video showed Breitbart yelling at [Occupy D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupy_D.C. "Occupy D.C.") protesters outside a Washington hotel hosting a [Conservative Political Action Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Political_Action_Conference "Conservative Political Action Conference") (CPAC). The video showed security escorting Breitbart back to the hotel while he told the protesters to "behave yourself", and alluding to reported assaults of women at Occupy encampments, he repeatedly yelled, "Stop raping people", and called the protestors "filthy, filthy, raping, murdering freaks!" David Carr said with the incident Breitbart had caused his last "viral storm on the Web."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-CPAC-49)

Breitbart appeared posthumously in _[Occupy Unmasked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupy\_Unmasked "Occupy Unmasked")_, a documentary film by [Steve Bannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Bannon "Steve Bannon") that contends that the [Occupy Wall Street movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupy_movement "Occupy movement") of "largely naïve students and legitimately concerned citizens looking for answers" is actually orchestrated by sinister, violent, and organized leaders with the purpose of not just changing, but destroying the American government.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-50)
