Breitbart described himself as "eighty-five per cent conservative and fifteen per cent libertarian".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-51) Breitbart had previously described himself as a Democrat but shifted towards being conservative after witnessing the Democrats' treatment of [Clarence Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas "Clarence Thomas") during his senate confirmation hearing.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-53)

Breitbart supported legalization of [prostitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostitution "Prostitution"),[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-54)[gay rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_Rights "Gay Rights"), and [drug liberalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_liberalization "Drug liberalization").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-55) He was an opponent of [multiculturalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiculturalism "Multiculturalism") and [political correctness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_correctness "Political correctness").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Beauchamp-56) Breitbart argued for US military intervention in [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba'athist_Syria "Ba'athist Syria"), [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), and [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") for humanitarian reasons. He was also a supporter of [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-57)

Breitbart was a proponent of the [Cultural Marxism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Marxism_conspiracy_theory "Cultural Marxism conspiracy theory") conspiracy theory, claiming there are academics attempting to undermine western culture.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Beauchamp-56)

### Breitbart Doctrine

The Breitbart Doctrine is the idea that "politics is downstream from culture" and that to change politics one must first change culture.

[Christopher Wylie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Wylie "Christopher Wylie"), a former employee of [Cambridge Analytica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Analytica "Cambridge Analytica") stated in an interview with _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_:

> The reason why he [Steve Bannon] was interested in this is because he believes in this idea of the 'Breitbart Doctrine', which is that if you want to change politics you first have to change culture because politics flows from culture. If you want to change culture, you have to first understand what the units of culture are, and the people are the units of culture. So, if you want to change politics, you first have to change people to change culture.

—Chris Wylie, 2018[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-58)

Breitbart considered this idea an important one and often spoke of it in interview or cited it in print.

## Personal life and death

Breitbart was married to Susannah Bean, the daughter of actor [Orson Bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orson_Bean "Orson Bean") and fashion designer Carolyn Maxwell, and had four children.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-huff-2)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Saad-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-AP-60)

At around 11:30 p.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_time_zone "Pacific time zone") on February 29, 2012, Breitbart collapsed on a street near his home in [Brentwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentwood,_Los_Angeles "Brentwood, Los Angeles"). He was rushed to [Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_UCLA_Medical_Center "Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center"), where he was pronounced dead at 12:19 a.m. on March 1, 2012.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-file-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-63) He was 43 years old.

An [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") by the [Los Angeles County Coroner's Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Coroner's_Office "Los Angeles County Coroner's Office") showed that he had [hypertrophic cardiomyopathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy "Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy") with focal coronary [atherosclerosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atherosclerosis "Atherosclerosis") and died from congestive heart failure, which had been diagnosed the year before.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-file-62)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-64)

### Tributes

[Rick Santorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"), [Reince Priebus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reince_Priebus "Reince Priebus"), [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney"), [Jonah Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Goldberg "Jonah Goldberg"), [Joel Pollak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Pollak "Joel Pollak"), [Sarah Palin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Palin "Sarah Palin"), [Matt Drudge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Drudge "Matt Drudge"), [Sean Hannity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Hannity "Sean Hannity"), [Michael Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Steele "Michael Steele"), [Tucker Carlson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucker_Carlson "Tucker Carlson"), [Glenn Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Beck "Glenn Beck"), [Rush Limbaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush_Limbaugh "Rush Limbaugh"), and [Newt Gingrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newt_Gingrich "Newt Gingrich") paid tribute to Breitbart.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-media_star-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-68) Santorum called Breitbart's death "a huge loss" that strongly affected him.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-media_star-65)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-69) Romney praised Breitbart as a "fearless conservative", while Gingrich remembered him as "the most innovative pioneer in conservative activist social media in America".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-media_star-65)

A special episode of _[Red Eye w/ Greg Gutfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Eye\_(talk\_show) "Red Eye (talk show)")_ aired the day after Breitbart's death as the host and panelists paid their tributes and showed clips from his appearances on the show.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-70)

**Andrew James Breitbart** ([/ˈ b r aɪ t b ɑːr t/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); February 1, 1969 – March 1, 2012) was an American [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States "Conservatism in the United States") journalist[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-c-span-1) and political commentator who was the founder of _[Breitbart News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breitbart\_News "Breitbart News")_ and a co-founder of _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-huff-2)

Breitbart played a central role in generating media coverage of the [Anthony Weiner sexting scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Weiner_sexting_scandals "Anthony Weiner sexting scandals"), the [firing of Shirley Sherrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firing_of_Shirley_Sherrod "Firing of Shirley Sherrod"), and the [ACORN 2009 undercover videos controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACORN_2009_undercover_videos_controversy "ACORN 2009 undercover videos controversy").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-3) Commenters such as [Nick Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Gillespie "Nick Gillespie") and [Conor Friedersdorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conor_Friedersdorf "Conor Friedersdorf") have credited Breitbart with changing how people wrote about politics by "show[ing] how the Internet could be used to route around information bottlenecks imposed by official spokesmen and legacy news outlets."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Atlantic1-5)

## Early life

Breitbart was born to Irish American parents in Los Angeles on February 1, 1969.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WAPO20120301-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-7) According to his birth certificate, his biological father was a folk singer. When he was three weeks old, he was adopted by Gerald and Arlene Breitbart, a restaurant owner and banker respectively, and grew up in the affluent neighborhood of [Brentwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentwood,_Los_Angeles "Brentwood, Los Angeles").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WAPO20120301-6) His adoptive family was [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews"); his mother had [converted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Judaism "Conversion to Judaism") to Judaism when marrying his father.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-wsj-9) Breitbart studied at [Hebrew school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_school "Hebrew school") and had a [Bar Mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_Mitzvah "Bar Mitzvah").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-10)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8)

Breitbart attended [Brentwood School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentwood_School_(Los_Angeles) "Brentwood School (Los Angeles)"), one of the country's top private schools, but did not distinguish himself, saying: "My sense of humor saved me".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8) However, he discovered that he loved writing, publishing his first comedic piece in the school newspaper, the _Brentwood Eagle_, analyzing the inequality in his high school's senior and junior parking lots: "One had Mercedes and BMWs, the other Sciroccos and GTIs".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8) Breitbart remembers his upbringing as apolitical, except in one instance: when the family's rabbi tried to defend [Jesse Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Jackson "Jesse Jackson") against charges of antisemitism after his "[Hymietown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymietown "Hymietown")" comment, his parents left the synagogue in protest.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-family-8)

> [Joel Pollak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Pollak "Joel Pollak") wrote about how (Breitbart's) life and fire extended to Judaism: 'Andrew was proudly, and playfully, Jewish. In the last days of his life he wondered openly about observing [Shabbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabbat "Shabbat"), even as he continued to tease me about not eating bacon and shrimp cocktails. More than once he burst into a Hebrew school song or parts of his [bar mitzva portion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_and_bat_mitzvah#Aliyah_to_the_Torah "Bar and bat mitzvah") while working at his desk across from mine – partly to amuse me and partly to entertain himself.'[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-jpost.com-11)

Breitbart would remain "proudly and playfully Jewish" throughout his life. The liberal-Left Jewish weekly, _The Forward_, placed him on their 2010 list of the top 50 most influential American Jews.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-jpost.com-11) Joel Pollak wrote: "He carried his faith as he carried all his convictions: with a lighthearted touch but a deep commitment."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-jpost.com-11) Breitbart later said of his profession: "I'm glad I've become a journalist because I'd like to fight on behalf of the Israeli people... And the Israeli people, I adore and I love."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-jpost.com-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-12)

While in high school, Breitbart worked as a [pizza delivery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizza_delivery "Pizza delivery") driver; he sometimes delivered to celebrities such as [Judge Reinhold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judge_Reinhold "Judge Reinhold").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-13) He earned a [BA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in [American studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_studies "American studies") from [Tulane University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_University "Tulane University") in 1991, graduating with "no sense of [his] future whatsoever."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-14) His early jobs included a stint at [cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_television "Cable television") channel [E! Entertainment Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E!_Entertainment_Television "E! Entertainment Television"), working for the company's [online magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blog "Blog"), and some time in film production.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-wsj-9) He was a Lincoln Fellow at the [Claremont Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claremont_Institute "Claremont Institute") in 2009.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-16)

Previously left-leaning in his politics, Breitbart changed his political views after experiencing "an [epiphany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphany_(feeling) "Epiphany (feeling)")" while watching the late 1991 [confirmation hearings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas_Supreme_Court_nomination "Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination") for Supreme Court justice [Clarence Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas "Clarence Thomas"), due to what he considered unfounded attacks on the part of liberals based on former employee [Anita Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Hill "Anita Hill")'s sexual harassment accusations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-17) Breitbart later described himself as "a [Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") conservative" with [libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarianism "Libertarianism") sympathies.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-c-span-1)

Listening to radio hosts such as [Rush Limbaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush_Limbaugh "Rush Limbaugh") helped Breitbart refine his political and philosophical positions, igniting an interest in learning that he had suppressed as a result of his distaste for the "nihilistic musings of dead [critical theorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_theory "Critical theory")"[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Righteous_Indignation,_p._36-18) that had dominated his studies at Tulane. In this era, Breitbart also read [Camille Paglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Paglia "Camille Paglia")'s book _[Sexual Personae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual\_Personae "Sexual Personae")_ (1990), a massive survey of Western art, literature and culture from ancient Egypt to the 20th century, which, he wrote, "made me realize how little I really had learned in college."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Righteous_Indignation,_p._36-18)

## Public life

### Authorship, research, and reporting

Breitbart has been lauded for his role in the "evolution of pioneering websites" including _[The Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Huffington\_Post "The Huffington Post")_ and _[The Drudge Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drudge\_Report "Drudge Report")_, and later, for _[Breitbart News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breitbart\_News "Breitbart News")_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-19) Journalists such as [Nick Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Gillespie "Nick Gillespie") and [Conor Friedersdorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conor_Friedersdorf "Conor Friedersdorf") have credited Breitbart with bringing new voices to debates about politics and culture. Breitbart told _[Reason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason\_(magazine) "Reason (magazine)")_ in 2004 that, after feeling ignored by existing outlets, "We decided to go out and create our media." Described as "a series of do-it-yourself demonstration projects" and "conversation pits", the Breitbart websites have been both criticized and praised for their role in various political issues.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Atlantic1-5)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Gillespie-20) Breitbart has been recognized for adopting an inclusive stance with regard to the participation of gay people in the conservative movement. He has also been credited with helping to derail [conspiracy theories about Barack Obama's citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama_citizenship_conspiracy_theories "Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Atlantic1-5)

In 1995, Breitbart saw _The Drudge Report_ and was so impressed that he e-mailed [Matt Drudge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Drudge "Matt Drudge"). Breitbart said, "I thought what he was doing was by far the coolest thing on the Internet. And I still do."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-huff-2) Breitbart described himself as "Matt Drudge's [bitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitch_(insult)#In_reference_to_men "Bitch (insult)")"[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-biyatch-21) and selected and posted links to other news wire sources. Later, Drudge introduced him to a then still-[Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)")Arianna Huffington[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-wsj-9) and Breitbart subsequently assisted in the creation of _The Huffington Post_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-22)

Breitbart wrote a weekly column for _[The Washington Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Times "The Washington Times")_, which also appeared at [Real Clear Politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Clear_Politics "Real Clear Politics"). Breitbart also co-wrote the book _[Hollywood, Interrupted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,\_Interrupted "Hollywood, Interrupted"): Insanity Chic in Babylon_ with [Mark Ebner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Ebner "Mark Ebner"), a book that is highly critical of U.S. [celebrity culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_culture "Celebrity culture").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-23) On January 19, 2011, the [conservative gay rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_conservatism "LGBT conservatism") group [GOProud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GOProud "GOProud") announced Breitbart had joined its Advisory Council.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-24)

In 2011, Grand Central Publishing released Breitbart's book _Righteous Indignation: Excuse Me While I Save the World_,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-25) in which he discussed his own political evolution and the part he took in the rise of [new media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_media "New media"), most notably at the Drudge Report and _The Huffington Post_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-27)

### _Breitbart News_

Main article: [Breitbart News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breitbart_News "Breitbart News")

Breitbart launched his first website as a news site; it is often linked to by the _[Drudge Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drudge\_Report "Drudge Report")_ and other websites. It has wire stories from the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press"), [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters"), [Agence France-Presse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agence_France-Presse "Agence France-Presse"), [Fox News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News "Fox News"), [PR Newswire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PR_Newswire "PR Newswire"), and [U.S. Newswire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Newswire "U.S. Newswire"), as well as direct links to a number of major international newspapers. Its political viewpoint as well as its audience runs to the [right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing "Right-wing") within the U.S. political spectrum.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-28) In 2007, Breitbart launched a video blog, Breitbart.tv.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-29)

In February 2011, Breitbart and one of his editors [Larry O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_O'Connor_(radio_host) "Larry O'Connor (radio host)") were sued for [defamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamation "Defamation") by [Shirley Sherrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Sherrod "Shirley Sherrod"), who had been [fired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firing_of_Shirley_Sherrod "Firing of Shirley Sherrod") after Breitbart posted a video of a speech given by Sherrod. The video had been selectively edited to suggest that she had purposely discriminated against a white farmer, while in reality the unedited video told the story of how she had helped that farmer.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Gerstein-31) Breitbart himself maintained that he stated this in his article about it, and that the purpose of the video was to show the crowd's positive reaction to Sherrod's statements about discriminating against the white farmer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-32) In July 2015, it was reported that Sherrod and Breitbart's estate had reached a tentative settlement.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Gerstein-31) It was reported October 1, 2016, that the lawsuit was settled.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-33)

In June 2011, Breitbart's websites broke the story that congressman [Anthony Weiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Weiner "Anthony Weiner") was [sending underage females revealing photographs of himself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Weiner_sexting_scandal "Anthony Weiner sexting scandal").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-34)

Since Breitbart's passing, under [Steve Bannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Bannon "Steve Bannon")'s leadership, _Breitbart News_ has become recognized as a [far-right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-right "Far-right")[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-FarRight-35) news and opinion website, which has been described as [misogynistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misogynistic "Misogynistic"), [xenophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenophobic "Xenophobic"), and [racist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism_in_the_United_States "Racism in the United States") by academics and journalists, notably The University of California Press.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-misogyny_xenophobia_racism-36)

### Commentaries

In 2009, Breitbart appeared as a commentator on _[Real Time with Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real\_Time\_with\_Bill\_Maher "Real Time with Bill Maher")_ and _[Dennis Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis\_Miller "Dennis Miller")_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-37) In 2004, he was a guest commentator on [Fox News Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News_Channel "Fox News Channel")'s morning show and frequently appeared as a guest panelist on [Fox News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News "Fox News")'s late night program, _[Red Eye w/ Greg Gutfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Eye\_(talk\_show) "Red Eye (talk show)")_. Breitbart also appeared as a commentator in the 2004 documentary _[Michael Moore Hates America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael\_Moore\_Hates\_America "Michael Moore Hates America")_.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-38)

On October 22, 2009, Breitbart appeared on the [C-SPAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-SPAN "C-SPAN") program _[Washington Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_Journal "Washington Journal")_. He gave his opinions on the mainstream media, Hollywood, the [Obama administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama "Presidency of Barack Obama") and his personal political views, having heated debates with several callers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-c-span-1)

In the hours immediately following Senator [Ted Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy "Ted Kennedy")'s death, Breitbart called Kennedy a "villain", a "duplicitous bastard", a "prick"[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-politico-39) and "a special pile of human excrement", adding, "Sorry, he destroyed lives. And he knew it," referring to Kennedy's actions during the [Chappaquiddick incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappaquiddick_incident "Chappaquiddick incident"), the [Robert Bork Supreme Court nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bork_Supreme_Court_nomination "Robert Bork Supreme Court nomination"), and the [Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas_Supreme_Court_nomination "Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-41)

In February 2010, Breitbart received the [Reed Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reed_Irvine "Reed Irvine")[Accuracy in Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accuracy_in_Media "Accuracy in Media") Award during the [Conservative Political Action Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Political_Action_Conference "Conservative Political Action Conference") in Washington, D.C. During his acceptance speech, he responded directly to accusations by _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ reporter Kate Zernike that [Jason Mattera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Mattera "Jason Mattera"), a young conservative activist, had been using "racial tones" in his [allusions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allusions "Allusions") to President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), and had spoken in a "[Chris Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Rock "Chris Rock") voice". From the podium, Breitbart called Zernike "a despicable human being" for having made such allegations about what, according to him, was just Mattera's Brooklyn accent.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-42) At the same conference, Breitbart was also filmed saying to journalist [Max Blumenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Blumenthal "Max Blumenthal") that he found him to be "a jerk" and "a despicable human being" over a blog entry in which Blumenthal accused Breitbart of employing a racist.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-43) Blumenthal was referring to [James O'Keefe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_O'Keefe "James O'Keefe") over his having attended a [Georgetown Law Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_Law_Center "Georgetown Law Center") discussion on race featuring Kevin Martin, [John Derbyshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Derbyshire "John Derbyshire"), and [Jared Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jared_Taylor "Jared Taylor"), the last of whom founded _[American Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Renaissance\_(magazine) "American Renaissance (magazine)")_, a white supremacist online magazine. Neither O'Keefe nor Breitbart endorsed Taylor's views.

In 2011, Breitbart said that "of course" [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") was not a conservative, adding:

> But this is a message to those candidates who are languishing at 2 percent and 3 percent within the Republican Party who are brand names in Washington, but the rest of the country don't know... celebrity is everything in this country. And if these guys don't learn how to play the media the way that Barack Obama played the media last election cycle and the way that Donald Trump is playing the election cycle, we're going to probably get a celebrity candidate.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WP.Aug.7.16-44)

These comments resurfaced after the controversy of Donald Trump hiring _[Breitbart News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breitbart\_News "Breitbart News")'_ executive chairman [Steve Bannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Bannon "Steve Bannon") to be his [White House Chief Strategist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Chief_Strategist "White House Chief Strategist").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WP.Aug.7.16-44)

### Activism

See also: [Tea Party movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_party_movement#Reports_of_slurs_at_health_care_reform_protests "Tea party movement")

Breitbart often appeared as a speaker at [Tea Party movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Party_movement "Tea Party movement") events across the U.S. For example, Breitbart was a speaker at the first National Tea Party Convention at Gaylord Opryland Hotel in Nashville on February 6, 2010.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-45) Breitbart later involved himself in a controversy over allegations of [homophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophobia "Homophobia") and [racial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism") slurs being used at a March 20, 2010, rally at the [United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol") in Washington, D.C., by asserting that slurs were never used, and that "it was a set-up" by [Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi") and the Democratic Party. Breitbart offered to donate $100,000 to the [United Negro College Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Negro_College_Fund "United Negro College Fund") "for any audio/video footage of the [N-word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigger "Nigger") being hurled," claiming that the several Congressmen made it up. Breitbart insisted Congressman [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis "John Lewis") and several other witnesses were forced to lie, concluding that "Nancy Pelosi did a great disservice to a great civil rights icon by thrusting him out there to perform this mischievous task. His reputation is now on the line as a result of her desperation to take down the Tea Party movement."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-AB-100402-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-WPost_Omb-47)

In February 2012, a YouTube video showed Breitbart yelling at [Occupy D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupy_D.C. "Occupy D.C.") protesters outside a Washington hotel hosting a [Conservative Political Action Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Political_Action_Conference "Conservative Political Action Conference") (CPAC). The video showed security escorting Breitbart back to the hotel while he told the protesters to "behave yourself", and alluding to reported assaults of women at Occupy encampments, he repeatedly yelled, "Stop raping people", and called the protestors "filthy, filthy, raping, murdering freaks!" David Carr said with the incident Breitbart had caused his last "viral storm on the Web."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-CPAC-49)

Breitbart appeared posthumously in _[Occupy Unmasked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupy\_Unmasked "Occupy Unmasked")_, a documentary film by [Steve Bannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Bannon "Steve Bannon") that contends that the [Occupy Wall Street movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupy_movement "Occupy movement") of "largely naïve students and legitimately concerned citizens looking for answers" is actually orchestrated by sinister, violent, and organized leaders with the purpose of not just changing, but destroying the American government.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-50)

Breitbart described himself as "eighty-five per cent conservative and fifteen per cent libertarian".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-51) Breitbart had previously described himself as a Democrat but shifted towards being conservative after witnessing the Democrats' treatment of [Clarence Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas "Clarence Thomas") during his senate confirmation hearing.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-53)

Breitbart supported legalization of [prostitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostitution "Prostitution"),[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-54)[gay rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_Rights "Gay Rights"), and [drug liberalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_liberalization "Drug liberalization").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-55) He was an opponent of [multiculturalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiculturalism "Multiculturalism") and [political correctness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_correctness "Political correctness").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Beauchamp-56) Breitbart argued for US military intervention in [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba'athist_Syria "Ba'athist Syria"), [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), and [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") for humanitarian reasons. He was also a supporter of [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-57)

Breitbart was a proponent of the [Cultural Marxism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Marxism_conspiracy_theory "Cultural Marxism conspiracy theory") conspiracy theory, claiming there are academics attempting to undermine western culture.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Beauchamp-56)

### Breitbart Doctrine

The Breitbart Doctrine is the idea that "politics is downstream from culture" and that to change politics one must first change culture.

[Christopher Wylie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Wylie "Christopher Wylie"), a former employee of [Cambridge Analytica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Analytica "Cambridge Analytica") stated in an interview with _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_:

> The reason why he [Steve Bannon] was interested in this is because he believes in this idea of the 'Breitbart Doctrine', which is that if you want to change politics you first have to change culture because politics flows from culture. If you want to change culture, you have to first understand what the units of culture are, and the people are the units of culture. So, if you want to change politics, you first have to change people to change culture.

—Chris Wylie, 2018[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-58)

Breitbart considered this idea an important one and often spoke of it in interview or cited it in print.

## Personal life and death

Breitbart was married to Susannah Bean, the daughter of actor [Orson Bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orson_Bean "Orson Bean") and fashion designer Carolyn Maxwell, and had four children.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-huff-2)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-Saad-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-AP-60)

At around 11:30 p.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_time_zone "Pacific time zone") on February 29, 2012, Breitbart collapsed on a street near his home in [Brentwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentwood,_Los_Angeles "Brentwood, Los Angeles"). He was rushed to [Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_UCLA_Medical_Center "Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center"), where he was pronounced dead at 12:19 a.m. on March 1, 2012.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-file-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-63) He was 43 years old.

An [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") by the [Los Angeles County Coroner's Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Coroner's_Office "Los Angeles County Coroner's Office") showed that he had [hypertrophic cardiomyopathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy "Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy") with focal coronary [atherosclerosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atherosclerosis "Atherosclerosis") and died from congestive heart failure, which had been diagnosed the year before.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-file-62)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-64)

### Tributes

[Rick Santorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Santorum "Rick Santorum"), [Reince Priebus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reince_Priebus "Reince Priebus"), [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney"), [Jonah Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Goldberg "Jonah Goldberg"), [Joel Pollak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Pollak "Joel Pollak"), [Sarah Palin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Palin "Sarah Palin"), [Matt Drudge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Drudge "Matt Drudge"), [Sean Hannity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Hannity "Sean Hannity"), [Michael Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Steele "Michael Steele"), [Tucker Carlson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucker_Carlson "Tucker Carlson"), [Glenn Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Beck "Glenn Beck"), [Rush Limbaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush_Limbaugh "Rush Limbaugh"), and [Newt Gingrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newt_Gingrich "Newt Gingrich") paid tribute to Breitbart.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-media_star-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-68) Santorum called Breitbart's death "a huge loss" that strongly affected him.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-media_star-65)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-69) Romney praised Breitbart as a "fearless conservative", while Gingrich remembered him as "the most innovative pioneer in conservative activist social media in America".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-media_star-65)

A special episode of _[Red Eye w/ Greg Gutfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Eye\_(talk\_show) "Red Eye (talk show)")_ aired the day after Breitbart's death as the host and panelists paid their tributes and showed clips from his appearances on the show.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Breitbart#cite_note-70)

_**Axios**_ (styled **ΛXIOS** in the logo) is an American news website based in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"). It was founded in 2016 and launched the following year by former _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")_ journalists [Jim VandeHei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_VandeHei "Jim VandeHei"), [Mike Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Allen_(journalist) "Michael Allen (journalist)"), and Roy Schwartz. The site's name is based on the [Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek "Ancient Greek")ἄξιος (_áxios_, lit.'worthy').[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2)

_Axios_ articles are often brief to facilitate quick reading; most are shorter than 300 words and use bullet points. In addition to news articles, _Axios_ produces daily and weekly industry-specific [newsletters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsletter "Newsletter") (including Allen's _Axios AM_, a successor to his newsletter _[Politico Playbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico\_Playbook "Politico Playbook")_ for _Politico_).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2)

In September 2022, [Cox Enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cox_Enterprises "Cox Enterprises") completed its acquisition of _Axios_ for $525 million.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-arlnow-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-4)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Axios_(website)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

VandeHei said he wanted _Axios_ to be a "mix between _[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_ and [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter")", which attracted criticism.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-5) The company initially covered a mix of business, politics, technology, health care, and media. VandeHei said _Axios_ would focus on the "collision between tech and areas such as bureaucracy, healthcare, energy, and the transportation infrastructure".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2) At its launch, Nicholas Johnston, a former managing editor at [Bloomberg L.P.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_L.P. "Bloomberg L.P."), was named its editor-in-chief.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:4-6)

In 2016, _Axios_ secured $10 million in a round of financing led by Lerer Hippeau Ventures. Backers include media-partner [NBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_News "NBC News"), [Laurene Powell Jobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurene_Powell_Jobs "Laurene Powell Jobs")'s [Emerson Collective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson_Collective "Emerson Collective"), [Greycroft Partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greycroft_Partners "Greycroft Partners"), and David and Katherine Bradley, owners of [Atlantic Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Media "Atlantic Media").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2) The company had raised $30 million as of November 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Axios_(website)&action=edit).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:3-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-8) It planned to focus on "business, technology, politics, and media trends".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2)_Axios_ generates revenue through short-form [native advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_advertising "Native advertising") and sponsored newsletters.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-9) It earned more than $10 million in revenue in its first seven months.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:3-7)

In January 2017, _Axios_ hired as an [executive vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_vice_president "Executive vice president")[Evan Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Ryan "Evan Ryan"), the [Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_of_State_for_Educational_and_Cultural_Affairs "Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs") and a former staffer for Vice President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:2-10)_Axios_ had 6 million unique visitors in September 2017, according to [Comscore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comscore "Comscore"). As of November 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Axios_(website)&action=edit), _Axios_ reported it had 200,000 subscribers to 11 newsletters, with an average [open rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_rate "Open rate") of 52 percent. The same month, it said it would use a new $20 million investment to expand data analysis, product development, fund audience growth, and increase staff to 150, up from 89.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:3-7)

In March and April 2019, _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_ and _[Wired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired\_(magazine) "Wired (magazine)")_ reported that _Axios_ had paid a firm to improve its reputation by lobbying for changes to the [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia "Wikipedia") articles on _Axios_ and [Jonathan Swan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Swan "Jonathan Swan").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-HuffPost-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-Wired-12)

In July 2020, under the [first presidency of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump"), _Axios_ received $4.8 million in federal loans from the [Paycheck Protection Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paycheck_Protection_Program "Paycheck Protection Program") for salary replacement during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). It later returned the money, with VandeHei explaining that the loans had become "politically polarizing".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-13) In September 2020, _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ reported that _Axios_ was on track to be profitable in 2020 "despite the economic turmoil stemming from the coronavirus that led to broad layoffs and pay cuts at many media outlets".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-14)

In May 2021, _The Wall Street Journal_ reported that merger discussions between _Axios_ and _[The Athletic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Athletic "The Athletic")_ had ended, with _The Athletic_ opting to pursue a deal with _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Company "The New York Times Company")_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-15)

On August 8, 2022, _Axios_ announced that it had been sold to [Cox Enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cox_Enterprises "Cox Enterprises") for $525 million. As part of the transaction, _Axios_ spun out [Axios HQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_HQ "Axios HQ") as a separate software company.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-NYTimesSold-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:0-17) According to the deal, Cox owns 70% of the company, while _Axios_ employees and its founders retain ownership of the remaining 30%.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-wapo-cox-1) The acquisition was completed the following month.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-arlnow-3)

Since 2021, _Axios_ has launched a network of local newsletters across the United States.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-18) The company has also focused on growing its events business.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-19)

In March 2023, _Axios_ fired Ben Montgomery, a [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") finalist, after he described as "propaganda" a [Florida Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Department_of_Education "Florida Department of Education") press release about an event hosted by Governor [Ron DeSantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_DeSantis "Ron DeSantis") "exposing the [diversity, equity and inclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity,_equity_and_inclusion "Diversity, equity and inclusion") scam in higher education".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-20)

In August 2024, _Axios_ laid off 50 employees, which amounted to 10 percent of its total staff.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-21)

## Content

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Axios_(website)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Content")]

_Axios_ content is designed for digital platforms, such as [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") and [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat"), as well as its own website.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2) Its articles are typically less than 300 words long, as most _Axios_ content is geared for quick, concise reads.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-22) In addition to its website, _Axios_ content is distributed via newsletters covering politics, technology, healthcare, and other subjects.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:1-23) Among the newsletters is a daily report by co-founder Mike Allen, who formerly wrote _Politico_'s _Playbook_ newsletter.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2) Some _Axios_ newsletters are free, while others are paid. The company sells a subscription service called _Axios Pro_ that bundles several paid newsletters, starting at $599 per year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:1-23)

_Axios_ reporters have made television appearances on NBC News and [MSNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSNBC "MSNBC") under an agreement with NBC, secured in 2017.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:4-6) Its [NBC Universal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Universal "NBC Universal") partnership has featured Allen on MSNBC's show _[Morning Joe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morning\_Joe "Morning Joe")_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-25)

In 2021, the documentary series _Axios_ on [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") won the News and Documentary [Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards") for Outstanding Interview for the interview with President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") conducted by [Jonathan Swan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Swan "Jonathan Swan").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-26)

In May 2026, a report by _[Press Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press\_Gazette "Press Gazette")_ revealed that _Axios_ had cut content output by 22% in the first quarter of the year, while traffic increased 30%, signaling a change in editorial approach.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-27)

_**Axios**_ (styled **ΛXIOS** in the logo) is an American news website based in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"). It was founded in 2016 and launched the following year by former _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")_ journalists [Jim VandeHei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_VandeHei "Jim VandeHei"), [Mike Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Allen_(journalist) "Michael Allen (journalist)"), and Roy Schwartz. The site's name is based on the [Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek "Ancient Greek")ἄξιος (_áxios_, lit.'worthy').[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2)

_Axios_ articles are often brief to facilitate quick reading; most are shorter than 300 words and use bullet points. In addition to news articles, _Axios_ produces daily and weekly industry-specific [newsletters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsletter "Newsletter") (including Allen's _Axios AM_, a successor to his newsletter _[Politico Playbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico\_Playbook "Politico Playbook")_ for _Politico_).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2)

In September 2022, [Cox Enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cox_Enterprises "Cox Enterprises") completed its acquisition of _Axios_ for $525 million.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-arlnow-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-4)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Axios_(website)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

VandeHei said he wanted _Axios_ to be a "mix between _[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_ and [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter")", which attracted criticism.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-5) The company initially covered a mix of business, politics, technology, health care, and media. VandeHei said _Axios_ would focus on the "collision between tech and areas such as bureaucracy, healthcare, energy, and the transportation infrastructure".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2) At its launch, Nicholas Johnston, a former managing editor at [Bloomberg L.P.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_L.P. "Bloomberg L.P."), was named its editor-in-chief.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:4-6)

In 2016, _Axios_ secured $10 million in a round of financing led by Lerer Hippeau Ventures. Backers include media-partner [NBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_News "NBC News"), [Laurene Powell Jobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurene_Powell_Jobs "Laurene Powell Jobs")'s [Emerson Collective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson_Collective "Emerson Collective"), [Greycroft Partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greycroft_Partners "Greycroft Partners"), and David and Katherine Bradley, owners of [Atlantic Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Media "Atlantic Media").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2) The company had raised $30 million as of November 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Axios_(website)&action=edit).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:3-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-8) It planned to focus on "business, technology, politics, and media trends".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2)_Axios_ generates revenue through short-form [native advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_advertising "Native advertising") and sponsored newsletters.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-9) It earned more than $10 million in revenue in its first seven months.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:3-7)

In January 2017, _Axios_ hired as an [executive vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_vice_president "Executive vice president")[Evan Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Ryan "Evan Ryan"), the [Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_of_State_for_Educational_and_Cultural_Affairs "Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs") and a former staffer for Vice President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:2-10)_Axios_ had 6 million unique visitors in September 2017, according to [Comscore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comscore "Comscore"). As of November 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Axios_(website)&action=edit), _Axios_ reported it had 200,000 subscribers to 11 newsletters, with an average [open rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_rate "Open rate") of 52 percent. The same month, it said it would use a new $20 million investment to expand data analysis, product development, fund audience growth, and increase staff to 150, up from 89.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:3-7)

In March and April 2019, _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_ and _[Wired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired\_(magazine) "Wired (magazine)")_ reported that _Axios_ had paid a firm to improve its reputation by lobbying for changes to the [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia "Wikipedia") articles on _Axios_ and [Jonathan Swan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Swan "Jonathan Swan").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-HuffPost-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-Wired-12)

In July 2020, under the [first presidency of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump"), _Axios_ received $4.8 million in federal loans from the [Paycheck Protection Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paycheck_Protection_Program "Paycheck Protection Program") for salary replacement during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). It later returned the money, with VandeHei explaining that the loans had become "politically polarizing".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-13) In September 2020, _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ reported that _Axios_ was on track to be profitable in 2020 "despite the economic turmoil stemming from the coronavirus that led to broad layoffs and pay cuts at many media outlets".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-14)

In May 2021, _The Wall Street Journal_ reported that merger discussions between _Axios_ and _[The Athletic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Athletic "The Athletic")_ had ended, with _The Athletic_ opting to pursue a deal with _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Company "The New York Times Company")_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-15)

On August 8, 2022, _Axios_ announced that it had been sold to [Cox Enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cox_Enterprises "Cox Enterprises") for $525 million. As part of the transaction, _Axios_ spun out [Axios HQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_HQ "Axios HQ") as a separate software company.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-NYTimesSold-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:0-17) According to the deal, Cox owns 70% of the company, while _Axios_ employees and its founders retain ownership of the remaining 30%.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-wapo-cox-1) The acquisition was completed the following month.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-arlnow-3)

Since 2021, _Axios_ has launched a network of local newsletters across the United States.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-18) The company has also focused on growing its events business.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-19)

In March 2023, _Axios_ fired Ben Montgomery, a [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") finalist, after he described as "propaganda" a [Florida Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Department_of_Education "Florida Department of Education") press release about an event hosted by Governor [Ron DeSantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_DeSantis "Ron DeSantis") "exposing the [diversity, equity and inclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity,_equity_and_inclusion "Diversity, equity and inclusion") scam in higher education".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-20)

In August 2024, _Axios_ laid off 50 employees, which amounted to 10 percent of its total staff.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-21)

## Content

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Axios_(website)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Content")]

_Axios_ content is designed for digital platforms, such as [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") and [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat"), as well as its own website.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2) Its articles are typically less than 300 words long, as most _Axios_ content is geared for quick, concise reads.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-22) In addition to its website, _Axios_ content is distributed via newsletters covering politics, technology, healthcare, and other subjects.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:1-23) Among the newsletters is a daily report by co-founder Mike Allen, who formerly wrote _Politico_'s _Playbook_ newsletter.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-VF1-2) Some _Axios_ newsletters are free, while others are paid. The company sells a subscription service called _Axios Pro_ that bundles several paid newsletters, starting at $599 per year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:1-23)

_Axios_ reporters have made television appearances on NBC News and [MSNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSNBC "MSNBC") under an agreement with NBC, secured in 2017.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-:4-6) Its [NBC Universal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Universal "NBC Universal") partnership has featured Allen on MSNBC's show _[Morning Joe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morning\_Joe "Morning Joe")_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-25)

In 2021, the documentary series _Axios_ on [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") won the News and Documentary [Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards") for Outstanding Interview for the interview with President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") conducted by [Jonathan Swan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Swan "Jonathan Swan").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-26)

In May 2026, a report by _[Press Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press\_Gazette "Press Gazette")_ revealed that _Axios_ had cut content output by 22% in the first quarter of the year, while traffic increased 30%, signaling a change in editorial approach.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website)#cite_note-27)

**Evan Clark Williams** (born March 31, 1972) is an American [internet entrepreneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_entrepreneur "Internet entrepreneur").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-EvWimsLATimes2013-2) He is a co-founder of [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter"), and was its CEO from 2008 to 2010, and a member of its [board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors") from 2007 to 2019.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-Forbes_profile-3) He founded [Blogger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blogger_(service) "Blogger (service)") and [Medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medium_(website) "Medium (website)"). In 2014, he co-founded the [venture capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital "Venture capital") firm Obvious Ventures. As of May 2025, his net worth is estimated at US$2 billion, according to _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-Forbes_profile-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Williams was born in [Clarks, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarks,_Nebraska "Clarks, Nebraska"), as the third child of Laurie Howe and Monte Williams.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-4) He grew up on a farm in Clarks, where he assisted with crop irrigation during the summers. He attended the [University of Nebraska–Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nebraska%E2%80%93Lincoln "University of Nebraska–Lincoln") for a year and a half, where he joined [FarmHouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FarmHouse "FarmHouse") fraternity, then left the school to pursue his career.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-NYT_Ev-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-WSJ_Twitter_Revolution-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early career")]

After departing from college, Williams took on various technology jobs and [start-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startup_company "Startup company") firms in [Key West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_West "Key West"), Florida, and in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas") and [Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"), Texas, before returning to his family farm in Nebraska. In 1996 Williams moved to [Sebastopol, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastopol,_California "Sebastopol, California"), in [Sonoma County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonoma_County "Sonoma County") to work for the technology publishing company [O'Reilly Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Reilly_Media "O'Reilly Media"). He started at O'Reilly in a marketing position, later becoming an independent contractor writing computer code, which led to freelance opportunities with companies including [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel") and [Hewlett-Packard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hewlett-Packard "Hewlett-Packard").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-WSJ_Twitter_Revolution-6) While working at O'Reilly, he also started a website called EvHead.com, where he first began blogging about his thoughts.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-8)

### Pyra Labs and Blogger

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Pyra Labs and Blogger")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/2001_webby_awards.jpg/250px-2001_webby_awards.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2001_webby_awards.jpg)

Williams at [Webby Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webby_Awards "Webby Awards") in 2001

Williams and [Meg Hourihan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meg_Hourihan "Meg Hourihan") co-founded [Pyra Labs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyra_Labs "Pyra Labs") to make project management software. A note-taking feature spun off as [Blogger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blogger_(service) "Blogger (service)"), one of the first web applications for creating and managing [weblogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weblog "Weblog").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-9) Williams coined the term "blogger" and was instrumental in the popularization of the term "blog".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-10) Pyra survived the departure of Hourihan and other employees, and was later acquired by [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google") on February 13, 2003.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-11)

In 2003, Williams was named to the [MIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology")[Technology Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_Review "Technology Review")[TR100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TR35 "TR35") as one of the top 100 innovators in the world under the age of 35.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-12) In 2004, he was named one of _[PC Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PC\_Magazine "PC Magazine")'_ s "People of the Year", along with Hourihan and Paul Bausch, for their work on Blogger.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-13)

### Odeo and Obvious Corporation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Odeo and Obvious Corporation")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Evan_Williams%2C_Web_2.0_Conference.jpg/250px-Evan_Williams%2C_Web_2.0_Conference.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Evan_Williams,_Web_2.0_Conference.jpg)

Williams at [Web 2.0 Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_2.0_Summit "Web 2.0 Summit") in 2005

Williams officially left Google on October 8, 2004,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-14) to co-found [Odeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odeo "Odeo"), a [podcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast "Podcast") company.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-15) In late 2006, Williams co-founded [Obvious Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obvious_Corporation "Obvious Corporation") with [Biz Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biz_Stone "Biz Stone") and other former Odeo employees, to acquire all previous properties from Odeo's former backers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-16) In April 2007, Odeo was acquired by Sonic Mountain.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-17)

### Twitter

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Twitter")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/TechCrunch50_Day_Two_Afternoon_-_Evan_Williams.jpg/250px-TechCrunch50_Day_Two_Afternoon_-_Evan_Williams.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TechCrunch50_Day_Two_Afternoon_-_Evan_Williams.jpg)

Williams at [TechCrunch50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechCrunch50 "TechCrunch50") in 2008

Among Obvious Corporation's projects was [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter"), a popular, free social networking and micro-blogging service. Twitter was spun out as a new company in April 2007, with Williams as co-founder, board member, and investor.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-18) In October 2008, Williams became CEO of Twitter, succeeding [Jack Dorsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Dorsey "Jack Dorsey"), who became chairman of the board.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-19)

By February 2009, [Compete.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compete.com "Compete.com") ranked Twitter the third most-used social network, based on their count of 6 million unique monthly visitors and 55 million monthly visits.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-Compete-20)

In October 2010, Williams stepped down from the CEO position, explaining that he would be "completely focused on product strategy," and appointed [Dick Costolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Costolo "Dick Costolo") as his replacement.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-21)

Following the announcement of Twitter's [initial public offering (IPO)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") in 2013, the company was valued at between US$14 billion and US$20 billion.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-22)

On April 6, 2017, an article announced Williams would sell 30 percent of his stock in Twitter, for "personal reasons."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-23)

In February 2019, Williams stepped down from his role as a board member of Twitter.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-24)

### Medium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Medium")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Web_Summit_2018_-_Press_Conference_-_Day_3%2C_November_8_SD5_9161_%2831913004358%29.jpg/250px-Web_Summit_2018_-_Press_Conference_-_Day_3%2C_November_8_SD5_9161_%2831913004358%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Web_Summit_2018_-_Press_Conference_-_Day_3,_November_8_SD5_9161_(31913004358).jpg)

Williams speaking at [2018 Web Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_Summit "Web Summit")

On September 25, 2012, Williams created the publishing platform [Medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medium_(website) "Medium (website)"). Initially, it was available only to early adopters, but was opened to the public in 2013.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-25)

On April 5, 2013, Williams and Stone announced that they would be unwinding Obvious Corporation as they focused on individual startups.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-26)

On July 12, 2022, it was announced Williams would step down as Medium's CEO and become the chairman of the board.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-EvWillMediumStepDownNYT2022-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-tc-12jul2022-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-medium-12jul2022-29)

### Obvious Ventures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Obvious Ventures")]

In 2014, Williams co-founded the venture capital firm Obvious Ventures with James Joaquin and Vishal Vasishth. The firm is focused on companies they believe can make a positive change in the world.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-31) Since its inception the fund has raised about $585 million—$123 million in its first round, $191 million in its second and $271 million in its latest round.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-32) In 2024, Williams announced his new company, Mozi, which is a private social network he co-founded with entrepreneur [Molly DeWolf Swenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_DeWolf_Swenson "Molly DeWolf Swenson"). Mozi has raised $6M from investors including Obvious Ventures, WndrCo and BBG Ventures.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-33)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Williams lives in the [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") area with his wife, Sara, with whom he has two children.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-35) He is a [vegetarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetarian "Vegetarian"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-WSJ_Twitter_Revolution-6) and has invested – through the Obvious Corporation – in a [plant-based](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant-based "Plant-based")[meat alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meat_alternative "Meat alternative"), [Beyond Meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyond_Meat "Beyond Meat").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-36)

## Views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evan_Williams_(Internet_entrepreneur)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Views")]

Williams has been quoted as having a philosophy that it is important to conserve time, do fewer things, and to avoid distractions.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-37)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Ev-Williams-2013.jpg/250px-Ev-Williams-2013.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ev-Williams-2013.jpg)

Williams speaking at [XOXO Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XOXO_Festival "XOXO Festival") in 2013

Williams presented at the 2013 [XOXO Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XOXO_Festival "XOXO Festival") in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon"), and explained his understanding of Internet commerce.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-Wired-38) During his XOXO session, Williams also likened the Internet to "a lot of other major technological revolutions that have taken place in the history of the world," such as [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Agricultural_Revolution "First Agricultural Revolution"), and asserted that the Internet is not a [utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia "Utopia").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-Wired-38)

After President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") credited his election win to the use of Twitter, Evan Williams stated that if true, he was sorry.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-chicagotribune-39) He also said that the internet is "obviously broken because it rewards extremes".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-chicagotribune-39) Williams told the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") that he was wrong to think that an open platform where people could speak freely would make the world a better place.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-chicagotribune-39) His musings about future business objectives include considerations about the effect of the Internet upon society.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ev_Williams#cite_note-40)
